title: Informal Conjecture (§1.2, Theorem 1.1 remarks)
statement_text: The threshold for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to be connected when $X, Y$ are independent random graphs in $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is determined by the isolated-vertex threshold: ``it seems that (as in the usual case of a binomial random graph) this local obstruction to connectedness tells essentially the whole story.'' Formally (the authors' conjecture): there exists an absolute constant $C>0$ such that if $p\ge Cn^{-1/2}$, then $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ is connected with high probability.
context_text: For simple graphs $X,Y$ on $n$ vertices, the friends-and-strangers graph $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ has as vertices all bijections $\sigma:V(X)\to V(Y)$, two bijections being adjacent if one is obtained from the other by a friendly swap: exchanging the images of the endpoints of an edge $\{a,b\}$ of $X$ such that $\{\sigma(a),\sigma(b)\}$ is an edge of $Y$ (people placed on the vertices of $X$, two people may swap positions if they stand on adjacent vertices and are friends in $Y$). $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph, $\mathcal{G}(K_{r,r},p)$ the random subgraph of $K_{r,r}$ keeping each edge with probability $p$, and 'with high probability' means with probability tending to 1. The authors prove that if $p\le(2^{-1/2}-\varepsilon)n^{-1/2}$ then $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ is disconnected with high probability, because it has isolated vertices, while if $p\ge\exp(2(\log n)^{2/3})n^{-1/2}$ it is connected with high probability; so the threshold is $n^{-1/2+o(1)}$. They conjecture that the gap is an artefact of the proof, stating formally in their concluding section that $p\ge Cn^{-1/2}$ suffices for some constant $C$, and also ask the finer hitting-time question: in the random graph process on pairs $(X_t,Y_t)$, is the first time $t_{\mathrm{conn}}$ at which $\mathrm{FS}(X_t,Y_t)$ is connected equal to (or $(1+o(1))$ times, or $O$ of) the first time $t_{\mathrm{iso}}$ at which it has no isolated vertices? They prove $t_{\mathrm{conn}}\le t_{\mathrm{iso}}\cdot n^{o(1)}$ w.h.p.

title: Open Question (§1.2, Theorem 1.4 remarks)
statement_text: Do the cutoff for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to avoid isolated vertices and the cutoff for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to have exactly 2 connected components coincide when $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$? That is, is $d_{r,r} = \lceil (3r+1)/4 \rceil$ for all $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$?
context_text: For simple graphs $X,Y$ on $n$ vertices, the friends-and-strangers graph $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ has as vertices all bijections $\sigma:V(X)\to V(Y)$, two bijections being adjacent if one is obtained from the other by a friendly swap: exchanging the images of the endpoints of an edge $\{a,b\}$ of $X$ such that $\{\sigma(a),\sigma(b)\}$ is an edge of $Y$ (people placed on the vertices of $X$, two people may swap positions if they stand on adjacent vertices and are friends in $Y$). $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph, $\mathcal{G}(K_{r,r},p)$ the random subgraph of $K_{r,r}$ keeping each edge with probability $p$, and 'with high probability' means with probability tending to 1. If $X$ and $Y$ are bipartite on $n\ge3$ vertices, a parity argument (relating the sign of $\sigma^{-1}\tau$ to how the bipartitions are matched) shows that $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ has at least 2 connected components, and $\mathrm{FS}(K_{r,r},K_{r,r})$ has exactly 2. For $r\ge2$, $d_{r,r}$ is the smallest nonnegative integer such that whenever $X,Y$ are subgraphs of $K_{r,r}$ (on its full vertex set) with minimum degrees $\delta(X),\delta(Y)\ge d_{r,r}$, $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ has exactly 2 connected components. The authors prove $\lceil(3r+1)/4\rceil\le d_{r,r}\le\lceil(3r+2)/4\rceil$; the bounds coincide unless $r\equiv1\pmod4$. The lower bound is the minimum-degree cutoff for $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ to have no isolated vertices; unlike the non-bipartite case (where the analogous $d_n$ satisfies $\frac35n-2\le d_n\le\frac9{14}n+2$ while isolated vertices already disappear at minimum degree $n/2$), this cutoff is essentially the connectivity cutoff, and in their concluding section the authors conjecture $d_{r,r}=\lceil(3r+1)/4\rceil$.
